---
name: ui-forge
description: Design and implement distinctive, production-ready UI/UX for websites, web apps, dashboards, landing pages, portfolios, commerce, mobile apps, and interactive product experiences. Use when creating or redesigning an interface; translating references into an original design system; improving responsive behavior, accessibility, motion, or visual polish; adding purposeful 3D or scroll storytelling; or validating a UI before delivery. Do not use for backend-only work or minor copy edits with no interface impact.
---

# UI Forge

Create interfaces with a clear point of view, working behavior, and evidence-based quality. Preserve the user's product intent and existing stack. Treat motion, 3D, and generated media as progressive enhancements—not automatic decorations.

## Operating contract

1. Inspect the current project, local instructions, attachments, and available capabilities before choosing a stack or tool.
2. Reuse the existing framework, design system, components, and package manager unless the user explicitly requests a migration.
3. Infer ordinary design decisions from the brief. Ask only when a missing choice would materially change scope, brand direction, platform, or cost.
4. Build the requested scope completely. Do not expand a single page into a full product, or reduce a requested app to a static hero.
5. Use real content and functional interactions. Do not leave dead links, fake controls, empty media boxes, or "TODO" placeholders in delivered work.
6. Keep external writes, paid generation, deployment, and destructive changes approval-gated by the user's request and host permissions.
7. Verify the result in the strongest way the environment supports. Never claim a visual, accessibility, performance, or device check that was not run.

## Phase 0 — Route the environment

Before designing:

- Read repository guidance and inspect relevant files, routes, dependencies, and existing patterns.
- Identify the output surface: codebase, standalone prototype, design specification, generated visual, or native/mobile implementation.
- Inventory capabilities by function rather than vendor name: filesystem, shell, browser/preview, screenshot, image input, image generation/editing, web research, and deployment.
- Read [tool routing](references/tool-routing.md) when media, browser automation, deployment, or constrained tooling matters.
- Read [framework routing](references/framework-routing.md) when selecting or adapting a web, native-mobile, or cross-platform implementation.
- Keep a capability unavailable if the host does not expose it. Do not invent tool calls or silently substitute a paid service.

## Phase 1 — Extract the brief

Derive and record:

- product and primary user goal;
- audience and trust level;
- target surfaces and required routes/screens;
- content hierarchy and primary action;
- brand inputs, references, constraints, locale, and RTL/LTR needs;
- desired mood and motion intensity;
- existing stack and delivery format;
- acceptance criteria and validation path.

If the user supplies visual references, extract principles—composition, rhythm, density, typography, color behavior, and motion language—then create an original result. Do not copy protected brand marks, distinctive illustrations, or an entire composition.

## Phase 2 — Establish design direction

Read [theme derivation](references/theme-derivation.md). Produce a compact direction before implementation:

1. one-sentence visual thesis;
2. one dominant composition idea;
3. semantic color tokens with checked text/background pairs;
4. typography roles and a resilient fallback stack;
5. spacing, radius, elevation, and motion tokens;
6. density and content-width rules;
7. light/dark behavior when required.

Use one primary accent and let hierarchy come from scale, spacing, contrast, and composition. Avoid default "AI purple gradient + floating cards" unless the brief genuinely calls for it.

## Phase 3 — Compose the experience

Choose references based on the surface:

- Marketing, dashboard, commerce, portfolio, or responsive web: read [layout blueprints](references/layout-blueprints.md).
- Native or mobile-first UI: read [mobile UI patterns](references/mobile-ui-patterns.md).
- Multi-page or whole-product scope: read [page templates](references/page-templates.md).

Define routes/screens, shared chrome, navigation model, state model, and responsive changes before styling details. Include loading, empty, error, validation, success, permission, and offline states when the product can reach them.

For RTL or multilingual products, use logical layout properties, test both directions, keep icons direction-aware, and avoid embedding text into imagery.

## Phase 4 — Plan media and iconography

Read [asset generation](references/asset-generation.md) only when the interface needs imagery, video, illustration, 3D, or a coherent icon family.

- Prefer user-provided brand assets and repository assets when they are usable and licensed.
- Use available image retrieval or generation capabilities only when allowed by the user and host.
- Ask before spending credits, generating many assets, or using a third-party service.
- Give every asset a purpose, dimensions/aspect ratio, loading behavior, accessible alternative, and fallback.
- Use procedural CSS/SVG/canvas art when it communicates the idea better or when media tools are unavailable.

## Phase 5 — Add motion and depth deliberately

Read [motion and 3D](references/motion-3d-playbook.md) when motion materially improves hierarchy, feedback, or storytelling. Use [signature scenes](references/signature-scenes.md) for one primary showpiece on a marketing surface.

Motion baseline:

- use short state transitions and clear feedback on interactive controls;
- add entrance/reveal motion only where it improves orientation;
- prefer `transform` and `opacity`; isolate paint-heavy effects;
- preserve native scrolling and input behavior;
- provide a useful reduced-motion state;
- remove perpetual motion that competes with reading.

Use CSS depth/parallax before WebGL. Escalate to [Three.js scroll worlds](references/threejs-scroll-world.md) only for an explicitly spatial narrative. A scroll world replaces the signature scene and must retain native, reversible page scrolling, a static fallback, readable DOM content, bounded GPU cost, and complete teardown.

## Phase 6 — Implement production behavior

- Use semantic HTML or native platform semantics.
- Keep components composable and data-driven; avoid monolithic generated files.
- Use tokens instead of scattered literals.
- Preserve existing architecture and conventions.
- Wire every visible control to a real route, state change, or clearly disabled state.
- Implement keyboard, focus, hover, active, disabled, busy, and error behavior.
- Keep secrets and provider credentials out of client code.
- Do not install dependencies unless they are necessary, compatible with the project, and allowed by the task.

Use bundled assets as starting references, not mandatory dependencies:

- `assets/tokens.css` — portable design-token foundation.
- `assets/motion-utils.js` — dependency-free browser motion helpers.
- `assets/particle-effects.js` — time-based, reduced-motion-safe canvas ambience.
- `assets/Hero3D.jsx` — React/CSS-depth hero reference.
- `assets/ScrollWorld3D.jsx` — React/R3F page-scroll world reference.

## Phase 7 — Verify and iterate

Read [visual QA](references/visual-qa.md). Run the applicable checks:

1. build, typecheck, lint, and relevant tests;
2. inspect the rendered UI at representative narrow and wide sizes;
3. check console/runtime errors and failed network/media requests;
4. traverse routes and exercise primary interactions;
5. keyboard-test focus order, dialogs, menus, forms, and dismissals;
6. check contrast, labels, landmarks, target sizes, zoom, reduced motion, and forced colors where supported;
7. test loading, empty, error, validation, and success states;
8. test RTL and localization expansion when relevant;
9. measure performance when the page uses heavy media, animation, or WebGL.

If visual inspection is unavailable, say so and perform code-level checks without pretending screenshots were reviewed. Fix failures within scope and rerun the affected checks.

## Phase 8 — Deliver or ship

For delivery, summarize what changed, what was verified, and any real limitation. Link or identify the actual artifacts and entry points.

Deploy only when the user asks. Before deployment, verify production configuration, metadata, social image, asset paths, error handling, and rollback path. Prefer the project's existing hosting workflow; otherwise select from the deployment capabilities actually available.

## Quality bar

A completed UI must satisfy all applicable items:

- The first viewport communicates product, audience, and primary action without explanation.
- Visual language is distinctive and consistent, not a collection of fashionable effects.
- Requested routes/screens and reachable states exist and work.
- Body text and controls meet WCAG 2.2 AA contrast; visible focus is never removed.
- Layout remains usable at 320px, 375px, 768px, and a wide desktop target appropriate to the project.
- Touch targets are at least 44×44 CSS px where touch is expected.
- Content survives 200% zoom and realistic text expansion.
- Images reserve space; noncritical media lazy-loads; video has a poster and does not autoplay audio.
- Reduced motion preserves content and task completion.
- Motion stays subordinate to comprehension and input latency.
- WebGL has a static fallback, DPR cap, context-loss path, offscreen pause/unmount, and resource disposal.
- No secrets, fake data claims, dead `#` links, broken assets, or hidden placeholder text remain.
